#2 terms

10-Percent Doubling Rule#

10-Percent Doubling Rule is a race-cube shortcut: the player on roll can generally double when their adjusted count is within about 10 percent of the other player’s count. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

8-9-12 Doubling Rule#

Players use 8-9-12 Doubling Rule to describe a race-cube guideline: double at about 8 percent behind, redouble at 9 percent, and take up to roughly 12 percent behind. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

A26 terms

ABT#

ABT stands for American Backgammon Tour, a series of tournament events in the United States. Players may see the abbreviation in tournament schedules, standings, and community discussion.

Category:

Ace#

Ace describes the number 1 on a die. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Ace-Point Game#

In backgammon, Ace-Point Game refers to a late holding game in which a player keeps the other player’s one-point and waits for a bearoff shot. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Acey-Deucey#

Also called: Binache, Catalin

In backgammon, Acey-Deucey refers to a family of backgammon variants, often associated with U.S. military play, in which 1-2 has special powers. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Acting Captain#

Acting Captain is used in a chouette. It is a temporary captain who makes the plays when the regular captain cannot act. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Action Play#

Action Play is a move intended to create contact, exchanges, or tactical complications. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Action Position#

Players use Action Position to describe a volatile position with many immediate tactical possibilities and large equity swings. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Active Builder#

In backgammon, Active Builder refers to a spare checker that can help make an important point on the next roll. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Advanced Anchor#

Players use Advanced Anchor to describe an anchor on the other player’s four-point or five-point. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Related lessons (2)
  • Opening Play Lab (Opening Play, Checker Play)
  • The Main Game Plans (Checker Play, Doubling Cube)

Advanced Level#

Players use Advanced Level to describe a tournament or teaching division for strong, experienced players below the top open level. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Ahead in the Count#

Ahead in the Count means having the lower pip count and therefore being ahead in the race. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Ahead in the Race#

Ahead in the Race means needing fewer total pips than the other player to bear off all checkers. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Ammunition#

Ammunition describes checkers positioned where they can attack blots or build points. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Analog Clock#

Analog Clock is a mechanical chess-style clock with hands rather than a digital display. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Anchor#

Also called: Holding Point

Anchor is a made point in the other player’s home board or outer board that gives safety and contact. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Annotated Match#

Players use Annotated Match to describe a recorded match accompanied by explanations of checker plays and cube decisions. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Annotation#

Annotation describes written or spoken analysis explaining decisions in a recorded game or match. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Anti-Joker#

In backgammon, Anti-Joker refers to an exceptionally unlucky roll that sharply damages a position. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Army#

Players use Army to describe a player’s full group of 15 checkers. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Around the Corner#

Around the Corner means movement from the other player’s outer board into the player’s own outer board. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Asset#

Players use Asset to describe a useful positional feature, such as an anchor, prime, strong board, or flexible builder. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Attack#

The action called Attack is to hit or threaten opposing blots, generally near or inside your home board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Attack Zone#

Attack Zone is the points on your side of the board from which checkers can support a blitz. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Attacking Game#

Players use Attacking Game to describe a game plan based on hitting, closing points, and keeping opposing checkers on the bar. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Automatic Doubles#

Also called: Automatic, Automatics

Automatic Doubles is an optional money-game rule that raises the initial cube value when both players roll the same opening number. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Awkward Number#

In backgammon, Awkward Number refers to a roll that cannot be played constructively and forces a positional concession. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

B45 terms

Back Game#

In backgammon, Back Game refers to a strategy based on holding two or more points deep in the other player’s home board and waiting for a late shot. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • The Main Game Plans (Checker Play, Doubling Cube)

Backgammon#

Also called: Triple Game

The term Backgammon refers to the game itself, or a triple-value win when the loser has borne off nothing and still has a checker on the bar or in the winner’s home board. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Related lessons (2)
  • Reading Positions and Engine Analysis (Engines and Analysis)
  • Why Is 25% the Basic Take Point When a Double Is Offered? (Doubling Cube)

Backgammon Board#

Also called: Board

Backgammon Board describes the playing surface with 24 narrow points arranged in four quadrants and divided by the bar. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Backgammon Server#

Players use Backgammon Server to describe an online service that hosts backgammon games, matches, ratings, or tournaments. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Baffle Box#

Players use Baffle Box to describe a device that randomizes dice by making them tumble through internal baffles before reaching the board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Bakelite#

Players use Bakelite to describe an early hard plastic sometimes used for vintage backgammon checkers and equipment. The term is mainly historical and may not be common in modern play.

Category:

Banana Split#

In backgammon, Banana Split refers to a very large split of the back checkers, typically exposing both as distant blots. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Bankroll#

Bankroll describes money set aside specifically for playing or wagering. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Bar#

Also called: Rail, Rim, Roof

The term Bar refers to the central divider where hit checkers wait until they can re-enter. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Bar-Point#

In backgammon, Bar-Point refers to a player’s seven-point, right away beside the bar. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Barabino#

Barabino is a traditional Italian tables game related to backgammon. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Battle of Primes#

In backgammon, Battle of Primes refers to a position in which both players have strong primes trapping opposing checkers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Bear In#

Also called: Bear On, Move In

The action called Bear In is to move all remaining checkers into your home board before bearing off. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Bear Off#

Also called: Bearoff, Go Out, Move Off, Off (the Board), Take Off, Throw Off

The action called Bear Off is to remove checkers from the board after all 15 are in your home board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Bearoff Database#

In backgammon, Bearoff Database refers to a precomputed table of exact or near-exact results for bearoff positions. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Beaver#

Also called: Beavers

Beaver is used in money play. It is an immediate redouble made by the player who accepts a double while keeping ownership of the cube. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Behind in the Race#

Also called: Behind in the Count

Behind in the Race means needing more total pips than the other player to bear off all checkers. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Bertha#

Bertha is traditional slang for the roll 6-3. The term is mainly historical and may not be common in modern play.

Category:

BIBA#

BIBA stands for British Isles Backgammon Association, a tournament and membership organization. Players may see the abbreviation in connection with organized backgammon in the United Kingdom.

Category:

Big Play#

Big Play is an aggressive play that accepts more immediate risk for greater positional gain. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Blitz#

Also called: Wipeout

In backgammon, Blitz refers to an attacking plan that repeatedly hits and closes home-board points to trap opposing checkers on the bar. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Related lessons (2)
  • Opening Play Lab (Opening Play, Checker Play)
  • The Main Game Plans (Checker Play, Doubling Cube)

Block#

Block means to restrict an opposing checker by occupying points in front of it. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Blockade#

In backgammon, Blockade refers to a connected group of made points that obstructs opposing checkers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Blocking Game#

Also called: Blocking Backgammon

In backgammon, Blocking Game refers to a strategy focused on building points or a prime in front of opposing checkers. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Blot#

Also called: Exposed Checker, Loose Checker

Players use Blot to describe a lone checker on a point, vulnerable to being hit. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Blot-Hitting Contest#

Players use Blot-Hitting Contest to describe a tactical sequence in which both players repeatedly hit exposed checkers. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Blue game#

In backgammon, Blue game refers to a collusive cheating arrangement in which players secretly cooperate against others. This term belongs in a rules, ethics, or historical explanation and should not be presented as acceptable conduct.

Category:

Usage note: Include only in an ethics or historical context, not as recommended conduct.

Blunder#

Players use Blunder to describe a large checker-play or cube error, often defined by analysis software as losing at least 0.080 equity. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Board Setup#

Also called: Board Layout, Layout

Board Setup describes the orientation of the board, points, checkers, bar, and bearoff trays for play. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Bold Play#

In backgammon, Bold Play refers to an aggressive move that leaves hittable blots to pursue a stronger objective. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Bot#

Players use Bot to describe a computer program that plays or analyzes backgammon. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Box#

Box is used in a chouette. It is the player competing alone against the team. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Boxcars#

Also called: Boxes, Boys (The Boys)

The term Boxcars refers to the roll 6-6. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Break a Point#

Also called: Break

Break a Point means to move one or both checkers away from a made point so it is no longer owned. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Break a Prime#

The action called Break a Prime is to open a point in a prime, allowing a trapped checker a possible escape route. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Break Contact#

Also called: Disengage, No Contact

Break Contact means to move all checkers past the other player’s checkers so no further hits are possible. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Break One's Board#

The action called Break One's Board is to open one or more made points in your home board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Broken Prime#

In backgammon, Broken Prime refers to a group of blocking points with at least one gap inside it. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Bronstein Clock#

Bronstein Clock is a game clock that restores up to a fixed delay after each move, so routine move time is not charged. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Build One's Board#

The action called Build One's Board is to make additional points in your home board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Builder#

Also called: Dilly Builder

Builder is a checker positioned to help make an important point on a future roll. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • Opening Play Lab (Opening Play, Checker Play)

Bury a Checker#

Bury a Checker means to move a checker deep onto a low home-board point where it has little future use. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Busted Back Game#

Busted Back Game is a mistimed back game whose anchors or checkers must collapse before a useful shot appears. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Bye#

Bye refers to automatic advancement in a tournament round without playing a match. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

BYOB#

BYOB stands for “bring your own board.” It is an instruction sometimes used for informal events. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

C58 terms

Calcutta Auction#

Players use Calcutta Auction to describe a tournament side auction in which participants bid for financial interests in players or teams. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

California Rule#

California Rule is a local chouette convention that allows a player to decline joining a cube decision under specified conditions. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Candlesticks#

Players use Candlesticks to describe an inflexible distribution with tall stacks on a few points and too few useful spare checkers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Captain#

Captain is used in a chouette. It is the team member who rolls the dice and makes the checker plays against the box. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Cash a Game#

Cash a Game means offering a double that the other player should pass. The game ends with the pass, and the doubler wins the value shown on the cube before the offer.

Category:

Catchers#

Catchers describes checkers placed to cover escape rolls or hit a runner trying to pass. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Centered Cube#

Also called: Cube in the Middle

Centered Cube is a doubling cube that still sits in the middle and belongs to neither player. Either player may offer the first double.

Category:

Championship Division#

Championship Division describes the highest-skill division in a tournament, also called the open or main division. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Chase#

Chase means to pursue a fleeing checker with the aim of hitting it. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Checker#

Also called: Chequer, Counter, Man, Piece, Stone

Checker is one of the 15 playing pieces controlled by each player. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Chouette#

Players use Chouette to describe a multiplayer format in which one player, the box, plays against a rotating team led by a captain. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Clean Play#

Clean Play is a move that improves the position without leaving unnecessary blots or awkwardness. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Clear a Point#

Clear a Point means to move every checker off a made point. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Clear from the Rear#

The action called Clear from the Rear is to move checkers first from the highest occupied points during bearoff or disengagement. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Client Software#

Client Software is the application a player uses to connect to an online backgammon service. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Clock#

Also called: Chess Clock

Clock is a timing device that limits each player’s thinking time. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Close Out#

Also called: Make One's Board, Shut Out

Close Out means to make all six home-board points while an opposing checker is on the bar. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Closed Board#

Players use Closed Board to describe a home board in which all six points are made. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Cluster Count#

Cluster Count is a quick race estimate that groups checkers into clusters rather than counting every pip separately. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Cock Shot#

In backgammon, Cock Shot refers to a roll or play that leaves an unexpected direct shot after appearing safe. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Cocked Dice#

Cocked Dice refers to dice that do not lie flat and must be rolled again under standard rules. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Coffeehouse#

Coffeehouse describes talk or behaviour intended to distract, pressure, or influence an opponent during play. This term belongs in a rules, ethics, or historical explanation and should not be presented as acceptable conduct.

Category:

Usage note: Include only in an ethics or historical context, not as recommended conduct.

Combination#

Also called: Combinations of the Dice, Dice Combination

The term Combination refers to the two numbers shown by a non-double roll. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Committed Position#

Players use Committed Position to describe a position whose checker structure strongly favours one game plan and offers little flexibility to switch. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Compact Position#

In backgammon, Compact Position refers to a position whose checkers are close enough to support and protect one another. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Confetti#

Players use Confetti to describe a scattered position with many loose checkers and little connection. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Confidence Interval#

Confidence Interval is a statistical range intended to contain a rollout’s true value with a stated level of confidence. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Connected Position#

Players use Connected Position to describe a structure in which checkers remain close enough to support one another and build points. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Connectivity#

Also called: Communicate, Communication

Connectivity describes the degree to which checkers are close enough to work together safely. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Consolation Division#

Consolation Division is a secondary tournament event for players eliminated from the main division. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Consolation Flight#

Also called: Sympathy Flight

Consolation Flight is one section or bracket of a tournament consolation event. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Consolidate#

The action called Consolidate is to reduce loose checkers and organize them into safer points or connected groups. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Consultation#

Consultation is discussion among chouette teammates about checker plays or cube decisions. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Contact Position#

Players use Contact Position to describe a position in which opposing checkers can still hit or block one another. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Contain a Checker#

The action called Contain a Checker is to prevent an opposing checker from escaping by blocking, attacking, or repeatedly hitting it. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Control the Cube#

The action called Control the Cube is to own the doubling cube and therefore hold the sole right to redouble. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Convergence Value (of a Rollout)#

The term Convergence Value (of a Rollout) refers to the value a rollout estimate approaches as the number of trials becomes very large. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Correspondence Games#

Correspondence Games refers to games played slowly through exchanged messages, with time to analyze each move. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Counterclockwise#

The term Counterclockwise refers to the direction of checker movement when the player’s home board is on the left. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Counterplay#

Counterplay refers to active threats or opportunities available to the side that is otherwise under pressure. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Coup Classique#

Players use Coup Classique to describe a classic bearoff tactic in which a forced ace leaves two blots exposed to a lone checker on the ace-point. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Cover a Blot#

Also called: Button up, Cover, Secure a Point

Cover a Blot means to place a second checker on a blot, making the point and protecting both checkers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Cramped#

Cramped refers to lacking useful space, spare checkers, or safe moves. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Crawford Rule#

Also called: Crawford Game

Crawford Rule applies in match play. The first game after either player reaches one point from winning the match is played without the doubling cube. Knowing the rule makes it easier to understand cube decisions near the end of a match.

Category:

Crew#

Crew describes the chouette players on the captain’s team against the box. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Crossover#

In backgammon, Crossover refers to a checker’s movement from one board quadrant to the next. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Crossover Count#

Crossover Count describes the number of quadrant boundaries your checkers must cross before all can bear off. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Crunch#

Also called: Crunched Position, Crunching Position

Players use Crunch to describe a forced collapse in which a player must break useful points or bury checkers because the position lacks timing. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Cube Action#

Also called: Cube Decision

Cube Action is a decision involving whether to double, take, pass, beaver, or redouble. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Related lessons (2)
  • The Doubling Cube (Doubling Cube)
  • What the Cube Is Really Asking (Doubling Cube)

Cube Play#

Also called: Cube Handling

Cube Play is the strategy and decisions involved in using the doubling cube. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Cube Provocation Play#

Cube Provocation Play is a checker play that intentionally creates volatility and may induce an opponent’s cube action. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Cube Reference Position#

Players use Cube Reference Position to describe a well-understood position used as a benchmark for estimating the correct cube action in similar positions. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Cubeful Equity#

Cubeful Equity describes expected value with future doubling-cube decisions included. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Cubeful Rollout#

In backgammon, Cubeful Rollout refers to a rollout in which the simulated players are allowed to use the doubling cube. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Cubeless Equity#

Cubeless Equity describes expected points or outcomes when all cube action is ignored. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Cubeless Probability of Winning#

Also called: CPW

The term Cubeless Probability of Winning refers to the chance of winning if the game is played to completion without using the cube. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Cubeless Rollout#

Cubeless Rollout is a rollout that plays every trial to completion without cube decisions. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Current Stake#

Current Stake describes the game’s present value after applying the doubling cube to the initial stake. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

D44 terms

Dance#

Also called: Air Ball, Fail, Fan, Flunk, Stay Off, Stay Out

Dance means to fail to enter any checker from the bar because all rolled entry points are blocked. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Dansk Backgammon Forbund (DBgF)#

Dansk Backgammon Forbund, usually shortened to DBgF, is the Danish Backgammon Federation. Players may see this name in connection with organized backgammon in Denmark.

Category:

Dead Checker#

Also called: Dead Man

In backgammon, Dead Checker refers to a checker buried so deeply in the home board that it has little value for attacking or building. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Dead Cube#

Also called: Frozen Cube

In backgammon, Dead Cube refers to a cube whose next value would already be enough to decide the match, so further redoubling has no practical value. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Dead Number#

In backgammon, Dead Number refers to a die number that cannot be played legally or usefully in the current position. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Deep#

Deep refers to far inside a player’s home board, generally on a low-numbered point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Deep Anchor#

Players use Deep Anchor to describe an anchor on the other player’s one-point or two-point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Deuce#

The term Deuce refers to the number 2 on a die. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Dice#

The term Dice refers to the two six-sided randomizers used to determine movement. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Dice Cup#

Also called: Cup

Players use Dice Cup to describe a cup used to shake and release dice. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Dice Manipulation#

Dice Manipulation refers to any attempt to control or influence a supposedly random dice result. This term belongs in a rules, ethics, or historical explanation and should not be presented as acceptable conduct.

Category:

Usage note: Include only in an ethics or historical context, not as recommended conduct.

Dice Mechanic#

Also called: Mechanic

Players use Dice Mechanic to describe a cheat skilled at manipulating dice or rolls. This term belongs in a rules, ethics, or historical explanation and should not be presented as acceptable conduct.

Category:

Usage note: Include only in an ethics or historical context, not as recommended conduct.

Dice Tube#

In backgammon, Dice Tube refers to a transparent or enclosed device that randomizes dice as they tumble through it. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Die#

Die is one six-sided cube marked from 1 to 6. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Digital Clock#

Digital Clock is an electronic game clock that can support time delays and precise countdowns. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Direct Range#

Players use Direct Range to describe a distance of one to six pips, reachable with a single die. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Direct Shot#

Also called: Direct Hit

Direct Shot is a chance to hit a blot with the number on one die. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Disjointed Position#

Disjointed Position is a position whose checkers are separated and cannot easily support one another. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Distribution#

Distribution means how a player’s checkers are spread among the points, bar, and bearoff tray. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Diversification#

Also called: Diversify

Diversification means arranging checkers so that many different future rolls play constructively. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Division#

In backgammon, Division refers to a tournament section grouped by skill, qualification, or entry level. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Double#

Also called: Double In, Double Out, Turn the Crank, Turn the Cube, Twist the Cube

Double means to offer to continue the game for twice its current value, or a roll showing the same number on both dice. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Double Bump#

Double Bump is a roll that permits two hits while also advancing the hitting checkers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Double Direct Shot#

Double Direct Shot describes two separate direct ways to hit, or two blots each exposed to a direct number. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Double Ducks#

Also called: Ducks, Quacks

The term Double Ducks refers to the roll 2-2. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Double Elimination#

In backgammon, Double Elimination refers to a tournament format in which a player is eliminated only after two losses. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Double Hit#

Double Hit means hitting two of the other player’s checkers in one turn. It describes an immediate tactical gain created by the roll.

Category:

Double Jeopardy#

Players use Double Jeopardy to describe a danger that can hurt on both the present roll and a later roll if not addressed. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Double Match Point#

Also called: DMP

Double Match Point is a game whose winner will win the match, regardless of gammon value or cube action. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Double Shot#

Double Shot describes two distinct hitting chances available on the next roll. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Doubles#

Also called: Doublets

Players use Doubles to describe a roll in which both dice show the same number, played four times. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Doubling Cube#

Also called: Cube, Doubler, Doubling Block

Players use Doubling Cube to describe a six-sided marker showing 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64, used to track the game’s value and cube owner. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Doubling on the Come#

Doubling on the Come describes doubling before the hoped-for improving roll arrives, based on the threat of that roll. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Doubling Window#

The term Doubling Window refers to the range of winning chances in which doubling is correct and taking may still be correct. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Down#

Down means movement from the midpoint into the player’s outer board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Draw#

The term Draw refers to the tournament bracket or the process used to assign opponents. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Drop Point#

Drop Point describes the winning-chance threshold below which accepting a double is no longer correct. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Drop-Take#

In backgammon, Drop-Take refers to a cube decision so close that passing and taking have nearly equal equity. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Dropper#

In backgammon, Dropper refers to an online player who deliberately disconnects or abandons losing games to avoid a recorded loss. This term belongs in a rules, ethics, or historical explanation and should not be presented as acceptable conduct.

Category:

Usage note: Include only in an ethics or historical context, not as recommended conduct.

Duplicate Dice#

Duplicate Dice is a rollout method that gives competing plays the same dice sequences to reduce random noise. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Duplicate Tournament#

Also called: Duplicate Backgammon

Duplicate Tournament is a format in which players face matching positions or dice sequences so results can be compared more directly. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Duplication#

Duplication means arranging threats so the other player needs the same dice numbers for several different good actions. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Dutch Backgammon#

Players use Dutch Backgammon to describe a traditional variant in which checkers begin off the board and enter before moving around it. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Dyscommunication#

In backgammon, Dyscommunication refers to a position where separated groups of checkers cannot easily connect or support one another. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

E19 terms

Early Game#

Early Game describes the opening phase, before the main structure and game plan are fully established. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Early-Late Ratio#

In backgammon, Early-Late Ratio refers to a race estimate comparing the value of pips saved early with pips saved late in bearoff. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Edge of a Prime#

Edge of a Prime describes the open point right away in front of the leading end of a prime. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Effective Pip Count#

Also called: EPC

In backgammon, Effective Pip Count refers to a race measure that adjusts the raw pip count for distribution and expected bearoff wastage. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Efficient Double#

Players use Efficient Double to describe a double offered near the other player’s pass point, maximizing the value of the cube decision. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Eject#

The action called Eject is to hit or force an opposing checker out of a useful point or area. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Elimination Format#

Players use Elimination Format to describe a tournament structure in which losses remove players from contention, right away or after a set number of losses. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Elo Ratings System#

Elo Ratings System is a rating method that updates players according to results and the relative ratings of their opponents. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

EMG Equity#

Also called: Equivalent-to-Money-Game Equity

EMG Equity describes equity converted to the scale of points expected in an equivalent money game. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

End Game#

End Game describes the late phase, generally involving bear-in, bearoff, final contact, or last cube decisions. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Enter#

Also called: Come In, Reenter

The action called Enter is to move a checker from the bar into an open point in the other player’s home board. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Equity#

Equity describes the expected value of a position, accounting for the probabilities and values of all possible outcomes. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

ER Backgammon#

In backgammon, ER Backgammon refers to a backgammon program associated with early work on error-rate analysis. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Error Rate#

Error Rate describes average equity lost through checker and cube mistakes, generally normalized per decision or per move. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Escape#

Escape means to move a runner out of the other player’s home board or past a blocking structure. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Establish a Point#

Establish a Point means to place two or more checkers on a point and thereby own it. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Eureka#

Players use Eureka to describe a traditional tables-game variant related to backgammon. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Extras#

Extras refers to additional cube decisions or side agreements used in some chouettes, such as extra cubes. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

eXtreme Gammon#

In backgammon, eXtreme Gammon refers to a commercial backgammon analysis and playing program, often abbreviated XG. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

F24 terms

Fast Board#

In backgammon, Fast Board refers to a bearoff structure that removes checkers efficiently with little expected wastage. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Favorite#

Favorite is the player or side judged more likely to win. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Fevga#

Fevga is one of the three main Greek Tavli games, played without hitting and with both players moving in the same direction. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

FIBS#

FIBS stands for First Internet Backgammon Server, an early online backgammon service and community. The name is important in the history of online backgammon.

Category:

FIBS Rating#

In backgammon, FIBS Rating refers to a player rating used on FIBS and based on match results, opponent strength, match length, and experience. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

FIBS Rating Formula#

FIBS Rating Formula describes the mathematical rule used by FIBS to update ratings after a match. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Field Goal#

Field Goal is slang for making the three-point, often by playing two checkers there. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Fighter's Bracket#

Fighter's Bracket is a secondary tournament bracket for players who lose in an earlier event. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Finalist#

Finalist is a player who reaches the final match of an elimination event. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Finals#

Finals is the last tournament round, which decides the winner. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Fischer Clock#

Fischer Clock is a clock that adds a fixed increment to a player’s remaining time after each move. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Fish#

Fish describes derogatory gambling slang for a weak or inexperienced player. This is dated and insulting slang, so it should be labelled clearly rather than used as ordinary teaching language.

Category:

Usage note: Dated and derogatory player slang; label clearly if retained.

Five-Point#

Also called: Cinque-Point

Five-Point describes the fifth point in a player’s home board, widely considered the most valuable home-board point. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Flexibility#

Flexibility is the ability of a position to use many future rolls constructively without major concessions. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

  • Opening Play Lab (Opening Play, Checker Play)

Flight#

Flight is a separate bracket or section within a tournament event. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Forced Move#

Also called: Forced Play

Forced Move is the only legal checker play available for a roll. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Forward Anchor#

Players use Forward Anchor to describe an anchor on a relatively high point in the other player’s home board or outer board. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Forward Game#

In backgammon, Forward Game refers to a strategy based on advanced anchors, forward points, and pressure rather than deep defensive holding. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Four-Point#

Also called: Quatre-Point

Four-Point is the fourth point in a player’s home board. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Free Drop#

Free Drop refers to at certain post-Crawford scores, the trailer’s option to pass an early double with little or no match-equity cost. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Freeze a Builder#

Freeze a Builder means to make a checker unavailable for point-making because moving it would expose or damage another feature. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Freeze-Out Match#

In backgammon, Freeze-Out Match refers to a match or series in which a fixed bankroll or stake is played until one side loses it. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Front a Prime#

Front a Prime means to place a checker or anchor directly in front of the other player’s prime. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Full Prime#

Full Prime means six consecutive made points, which no opposing checker can jump in one roll. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

G23 terms

Gain a Tempo#

The action called Gain a Tempo is to use a hit or forcing move to make the other player lose part of a turn. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Game Plan#

Game Plan is the broad strategy suited to the position, such as racing, priming, blitzing, holding, or playing a back game. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Game Winning Chances#

Also called: GWC

Game Winning Chances is the probability of winning the current game, generally before considering cube value. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Gamesmanship#

Gamesmanship refers to conduct intended to gain a competitive edge through pressure or distraction rather than better play. This term belongs in a rules, ethics, or historical explanation and should not be presented as acceptable conduct.

Category:

Usage note: Include only in an ethics or historical context, not as recommended conduct.

Gammon#

Also called: Double Game

Players use Gammon to describe a double-value win in which the loser has not borne off any checker. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Gammon Count#

In backgammon, Gammon Count refers to an estimate of the rolls or crossovers each side needs in a gammon-saving or gammon-winning race. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Gammon Cube#

In backgammon, Gammon Cube refers to a teaching or analysis device used to compare the value of gammons with ordinary wins and losses. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Gammon Price#

The term Gammon Price refers to the value of winning a gammon relative to winning a single game at a particular match score. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Gammon Rate#

Gammon Rate describes the proportion of wins that are gammons, often expressed as a percentage. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Gammon Vigorish (Vig)#

Gammon Vigorish (Vig) describes extra equity created by meaningful gammon chances beyond ordinary game-winning chances. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Gammon-Go#

Also called: GG

Players use Gammon-Go to describe a match-score situation where winning a gammon is unusually valuable and losing one costs little or nothing extra. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Gammon-Save#

Also called: GS

Players use Gammon-Save to describe a match-score situation where avoiding a gammon loss is unusually important. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Gammonish#

Gammonish refers to describing a position with substantial gammon chances. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Gap#

Gap is an unmade point inside a group of made points or a prime. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Gin Position#

Gin Position is a position from which victory is certain with correct play, regardless of future rolls. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Gioul#

Gioul is a Middle Eastern tables-game variant related to backgammon. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Give a Little Present to#

Give a Little Present to refers to old gambling slang for intentionally giving an opponent a favourable concession or chance. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Giving for Game#

Giving for Game is a settlement convention in which a player offers points in exchange for treating the game as complete. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

GNU Backgammon#

In backgammon, GNU Backgammon refers to a free, open-source backgammon program for play, analysis, rollouts, and match records. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Golden Point#

Golden Point describes the five-point in either player’s home board. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Greedy Bearoff#

In backgammon, Greedy Bearoff refers to a bearoff play that removes the maximum number of checkers right away, possibly at the cost of future efficiency. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Guff (Guffy)#

Guff (Guffy) is traditional slang for the roll 5-4. The term is mainly historical and may not be common in modern play.

Category:

Gul Bara#

Gul Bara is a tables-game variant in which both players move in the same direction and cannot hit. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

H16 terms

Half a Roll#

Half a Roll is one player-turn, used as a unit of timing or development. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Half-Crossover Method#

In backgammon, Half-Crossover Method refers to a quick bearoff estimate that counts approximate half-board movements instead of every pip. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Handicap#

Players use Handicap to describe an adjustment to score, odds, time, or conditions intended to balance players of different strengths. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Head-to-Head#

In backgammon, Head-to-Head refers to a format or comparison involving the same two players directly against each other. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Heavy Point#

Heavy Point is a point holding four or more checkers, often creating inflexibility. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Hedge#

In backgammon, Hedge refers to a side agreement or opposing wager used to reduce financial risk from an uncertain result. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Hit#

Also called: Bump, Knock Off, Pick Up, Send Back, Take Up

Hit means to land on an opposing blot and place that checker on the bar. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Hit and Cover#

Hit and Cover means hitting one of the other player’s blots with part of the roll and covering one of your own blots with the rest. The move combines an attack with an immediate improvement in safety.

Category:

Hit and Split#

Hit and Split means to hit a blot while also splitting the back checkers or breaking an anchor. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Hit Off the Edge of a Prime#

The action called Hit Off the Edge of a Prime is to hit a checker sitting just in front of your prime, generally to maintain control of the escape point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Holding Game#

Players use Holding Game to describe a strategy based on keeping an anchor and waiting for the other player to leave a shot while clearing points. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Holland Rule#

Players use Holland Rule to describe a former optional match rule that restricted doubling right away after the Crawford game. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Home Board#

Also called: Home, Inner Board, Inner Table

The term Home Board refers to the six-point quadrant into which all your checkers must move before you can bear off. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Horizon#

The term Horizon refers to the number of plies a truncated rollout or search examines before using an evaluation. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Hustler#

In backgammon, Hustler refers to a strong player who hides or understates their ability to obtain favourable gambling action. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Hyper-Backgammon#

Hyper-Backgammon is a fast variant in which each player starts with three checkers on the first three opposing home-board points. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

I12 terms

Illegal Move#

Also called: Illegal Play

Players use Illegal Move to describe a checker play that does not follow the dice or movement rules. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Illegal Moves Rule#

Players use Illegal Moves Rule to describe a rule requiring an illegal move to be corrected when noticed before the next valid roll. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Illegal Position#

Illegal Position is a board arrangement that could not result from legal play or does not match the recorded state. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Inactive Builder#

Inactive Builder is a checker that appears available but cannot safely or legally help make a useful point. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Indirect Hit#

Players use Indirect Hit to describe a hit made by combining both dice with one checker. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Indirect Shot#

Also called: Combination Shot, Fly Shot

Indirect Shot is a chance to hit that requires the combined value of both dice rather than one die alone. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Initial Double#

Initial Double describes the first voluntary use of the doubling cube in a game. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Initial Stake#

The term Initial Stake refers to the value assigned to the game before any doubles. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Initiative#

The term Initiative refers to the ability to make threats that force the other player to respond. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Intermediate Division#

Players use Intermediate Division to describe a tournament section for players between novice and open or championship strength. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Intermediate Level#

Intermediate Level is a learning or competition level beyond beginner but below advanced play. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Irish#

Irish is an optional variant in which doubles are played only twice rather than four times. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

J12 terms

Jackpot#

In backgammon, Jackpot refers to a generally single-elimination side event with a separate entry fee and prize pool. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Jacoby Paradox#

In backgammon, Jacoby Paradox refers to a cube situation where being allowed to double can alter checker play or equity in a counterintuitive way. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Jacoby Rule#

Jacoby Rule is used in money play. Gammons and backgammons count only after one player has turned the doubling cube. The rule changes the value of playing on for extra points before the cube has been used.

Category:

Jacquet#

In backgammon, Jacquet refers to a French tables game in which all checkers move in the same direction and enter before advancing. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Janowski's Formula#

In backgammon, Janowski's Formula refers to a shortcut for estimating match-winning chances from the score and points still needed. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Janowski's Formulas#

Janowski's Formulas is a family of formulas that estimate cubeful equity from cubeless results and assumed cube efficiency. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Janowski's Takepoint Formula#

In backgammon, Janowski's Takepoint Formula refers to a formula that estimates a player’s practical take point by accounting for cube ownership and efficiency. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Jellyfish#

Jellyfish is an influential commercial backgammon program built with a neural network and released in the 1990s. It played an important role in the development of computer backgammon.

Category:

Jeopardy#

Jeopardy refers to exposure to rolls that can cause immediate or future damage. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Joint Standard Deviation#

Also called: JSD

Joint Standard Deviation describes the estimated statistical uncertainty in the difference between two rollout results. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Joker#

Players use Joker to describe an unusually strong or lucky roll that greatly improves a position. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Junior#

In backgammon, Junior refers to a youth tournament category or a young competitor. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

K8 terms

Kauder Paradox#

Players use Kauder Paradox to describe a race-cube paradox showing that a position can become a correct double after a play that reduces winning chances. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Keith Count#

Players use Keith Count to describe a race-cube count that adjusts pip count for checker distribution, wastage, and the player on roll. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Key Point#

Key Point is a strategically important point whose ownership strongly affects the position. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Kibitz#

The action called Kibitz is to watch a game, sometimes while making comments. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Kibitzer#

Kibitzer is a spectator who watches and may comment on a game or match. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Kill a Checker#

The action called Kill a Checker is to bury a checker on a low home-board point where it has little future use. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Kill a Number#

The action called Kill a Number is to arrange the position so a particular future die number cannot be played or causes less damage. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Kleinman Doubling Formula#

Kleinman Doubling Formula is a race formula that estimates winning chances from the players’ pip counts and their difference. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

L20 terms

Ladder#

In backgammon, Ladder refers to a competition format in which players challenge nearby opponents to move up a ranking list. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Last Call for Breakfast#

Last Call for Breakfast is humorous tournament slang announcing the last opportunity to enter a consolation or side event. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Last Chance Event#

Also called: Last Chance Flight

Players use Last Chance Event to describe a final secondary tournament opportunity for players eliminated from earlier brackets. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Last Roll Position#

Last Roll Position is a position in which the next roll determines the game’s outcome. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Latto Paradox#

Players use Latto Paradox to describe a cube paradox in which an apparently stronger positional feature can reduce the practical value of doubling. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Leader#

Leader is the player ahead in match score or race. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Leave a Shot#

Leave a Shot means to make a play that exposes a blot to one or more hitting rolls. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Legal Move#

Also called: Legal Play

In backgammon, Legal Move refers to a checker play that uses the dice and follows all movement rules. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Legal Moves Rule#

Legal Moves Rule is a rule requiring players to correct all noticed illegal moves rather than allowing them to stand. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Liability#

In backgammon, Liability refers to a positional weakness or checker that may become costly, such as a blot, gap, or trapped runner. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Liby's Rule#

In backgammon, Liby's Rule refers to a race-cube rule of thumb based on adjusted pip counts and percentage differences. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Lipped Cup#

Players use Lipped Cup to describe a dice cup with internal ridges that help tumble and randomize the dice. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Live-Cube Rollout#

In backgammon, Live-Cube Rollout refers to a cubeful rollout in which both sides may double and redouble according to the simulated strategy. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Loaded Dice#

Loaded Dice means altered or weighted dice designed to produce unfair results. This term belongs in a rules, ethics, or historical explanation and should not be presented as acceptable conduct.

Category:

Usage note: Include only in an ethics or historical context, not as recommended conduct.

Long Backgammon#

Also called: LongGammon

Long Backgammon is a family of variants in which players generally move in the same direction and hitting rules differ from standard backgammon. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Loose Hit#

Also called: Hit Loose, Loose Play

Loose Hit means to hit in your home board without covering the hitting checker, leaving it exposed. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Lose One's Market#

Lose One's Market means to wait too long to double, then improve so much that the other player correctly passes. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Lover's Leap#

The term Lover's Leap refers to the opening play 24/13 with a roll of 6-5. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Luck Factor#

Luck Factor is an estimate of how much dice results helped or hurt a player relative to average rolls. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Luck Reduction#

Players use Luck Reduction to describe a rollout technique that adjusts trial results for estimated dice luck to reduce variance. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

M43 terms

Made Point#

Players use Made Point to describe a point occupied by two or more of your checkers and closed to the other player. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Magriel's Safe-Bold Criteria#

Also called: Bold-Safe Criteria, Safe-Bold Criteria

Magriel's Safe-Bold Criteria is a checklist for choosing between safe and bold plays based on board strength, anchors, threats, and race position. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Main Division#

Main Division is the primary tournament bracket, often the highest-skill or largest-prize event. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Main Flight#

In backgammon, Main Flight refers to a section of the main tournament event. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Major Split#

Major Split means moving a back checker several points forward, often from the 24-point to the 20-point or 21-point. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Make a Point#

Also called: Book a Checker, Close a Point, Lock Up a Point

Make a Point means to place two or more checkers on a point so the other player cannot land there. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Man in the Box#

Man in the Box is the box player in a chouette, playing alone against the team. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Mandatory Beavers#

In backgammon, Mandatory Beavers refers to a chouette or money-game rule requiring a player to beaver certain accepted doubles. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Mandatory Double#

Mandatory Double is a double with no downside at the match score, so it should be offered at the first legal opportunity. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Mandatory Extras#

In backgammon, Mandatory Extras refers to a chouette rule requiring team members to accept specified additional cubes or side actions. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Mandatory Take#

Players use Mandatory Take to describe a cube offer that must be accepted because passing would lose more equity, often by a large margin. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Manny Wong Proposition#

Players use Manny Wong Proposition to describe a named proposition involving repeated play from a specific position under agreed odds or scoring. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Market (for a Double)#

The term Market (for a Double) refers to the range in which the other player would still accept a double. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Market Gainer#

In backgammon, Market Gainer refers to a roll sequence that moves a position from no double into the correct doubling window. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Market Loser#

Players use Market Loser to describe a roll sequence that improves a position so much that an opponent who could take now must pass afterward. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Market Losing Sequence#

Market Losing Sequence refers to any sequence of rolls that causes the doubler to lose the opportunity to have a double accepted. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Match#

Match is a series of games played until one player reaches a fixed target score. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Match Equity#

Match Equity describes the probability of winning the match from the current score and situation. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Match Equity Table#

Also called: MET

In backgammon, Match Equity Table refers to a table of match-winning chances for different scores and cube outcomes. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Match Play#

Match Play is backgammon played to a fixed number of points rather than for a value per game. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.
