Match Winning Chances#

Also called: MWC

Match Winning Chances describes the probability of winning the entire match, generally expressed as a percentage. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Material#

The term Material refers to the checkers and made points that provide tangible positional resources. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Mechanical Play#

Mechanical Play is a move chosen by habit or a memorized rule without enough attention to the actual position. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Mental Shift#

Mental Shift is the adjustment from evaluating one type of position or score to another, especially after cube action. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Mexican Backgammon#

In backgammon, Mexican Backgammon refers to a backgammon variant with special rules for doubles and cube escalation. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Meyer Dice Tube#

In backgammon, Meyer Dice Tube refers to a compact dice-randomizing tube developed for backgammon play. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Mid-Point#

Also called: Comfort Station

Players use Mid-Point to describe a player’s 13-point, where five checkers begin the game. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Middle Game#

Middle Game is the phase after the opening when the main game plans and structures are established. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Minor Split#

Minor Split means moving one back checker a short distance forward, often from the 24-point to the 22-point or 23-point. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Misere#

Players use Misere to describe a variant or scoring condition in which the normal objective is reversed. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Mixed Roll#

Players use Mixed Roll to describe a roll showing two different numbers. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Mobility#

Mobility is the number and quality of legal, constructive moves available to a position. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Modern Backgammon#

Modern Backgammon describes contemporary theory shaped by computer analysis, emphasizing equity, cube action, and position types. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Money Management#

Money Management refers to controlling stakes and bankroll risk to avoid losses beyond an acceptable level. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Money Play#

Also called: Money Game Play, Stakes Play

Money Play refers to games scored by the cube value and optional gammons or backgammons, rather than by a target match score. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Monte Carlo#

In backgammon, Monte Carlo refers to a famous international tournament location, or simulation by repeated random trials depending on context. The term is mainly historical and may not be common in modern play.

Category:

Motif#

Players use Motif to describe a recurring tactical or strategic pattern that can be recognized across different positions. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Moultezim#

Players use Moultezim to describe a Turkish tables-game variant in which players move in the same direction and generally do not hit. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Move#

Players use Move to describe a player’s checker play for one roll, or the act of advancing a checker. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Move Down#

The action called Move Down is to move checkers from the midpoint into the outer board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Move Out#

The action called Move Out is to move checkers out of the other player’s home board or another contained area. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Move Up#

The action called Move Up is to advance a back checker to a higher anchor or forward point in the other player’s board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Mutual Holding Game#

Players use Mutual Holding Game to describe a position in which both players hold advanced points and wait for the other to leave a shot. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

N20 terms

N-Point Board#

Players use N-Point Board to describe a model or database restricted to positions with checkers on a specified number of home-board points. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

N-Roll Position#

Players use N-Roll Position to describe a race or bearoff position expected to finish in about N rolls. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Nack Blitz#

In backgammon, Nack Blitz refers to an aggressive opening and early-game blitz structure associated with Nack Ballard. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Nackgammon#

Nackgammon is a backgammon variant with a modified starting position designed to create more contact and complex play. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Nactation#

In backgammon, Nactation refers to a compact notation system for recording backgammon checker plays. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Narde#

Narde is a family of traditional race-style tables games in which both players move in the same direction. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Neil's Numbers#

Neil's Numbers is a simple set of match-equity estimates based on the number of points each player still needs. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Neural Network (Neural Net)#

Also called: NN

Players use Neural Network (Neural Net) to describe a machine-learning model that evaluates positions by combining learned numerical features through connected layers. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Next#

Next is a chouette term for the player scheduled to become captain or box after the current game. The term gives players a shared way to talk about the order of play.

Category:

No Dice#

Players use No Dice to describe an expression meaning a desired roll or legal move is unavailable. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

No-Brainer#

Players use No-Brainer to describe a decision considered so clear that little calculation is required. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Noncommitted Position#

Players use Noncommitted Position to describe a flexible position that can still develop into several different game plans. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Nonprogressive Consolation#

Nonprogressive Consolation is a consolation format in which all entrants begin together rather than joining at different stages. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Norges Backgammonforbund (NBGF)#

Norges Backgammonforbund (NBGF) describes the Norwegian Backgammon Federation. Players may see this name in connection with tournaments, membership, or the wider backgammon community.

Category:

Normal Game#

Normal Game refers to standard backgammon played with the usual starting position and rules. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Normalized Match Score#

Players use Normalized Match Score to describe a score expressed by points each player needs to win, such as 3-away, 5-away. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Notation#

Notation is a written system for recording rolls, checker moves, cube actions, and match scores. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Novice Division#

Novice Division is a tournament section intended for new or less experienced players. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Novice Level#

In backgammon, Novice Level refers to a beginner stage of learning or competition. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Nullo Play#

Players use Nullo Play to describe a form or variant in which the usual goal or scoring is reversed. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

O26 terms

Odds#

Odds is a numerical comparison of the likelihoods of different outcomes, or terms offered to balance a wager. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

On Roll#

The term On Roll refers to the player whose turn it is to roll and move. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

On the Bar#

Also called: In the Air, Two on the Roof

On the Bar means having one or more hit checkers waiting to re-enter. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

On Tilt#

On Tilt refers to playing emotionally and making riskier or poorer decisions after frustration or losses. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

One-Checker Model#

In backgammon, One-Checker Model refers to a simplified race model that replaces a full checker distribution with one representative checker. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

One-Point#

Also called: Ace-Point

The term One-Point refers to the lowest point in a player’s home board, also called the ace-point. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

One-Point Match#

One-Point Match is a match consisting of a single game with no cube action and no strategic value from gammons. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

One-Sided Bearoff Database#

In backgammon, One-Sided Bearoff Database refers to a database giving exact bearoff results for one player’s checker distribution without modeling an opposing distribution. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Online Backgammon#

Online Backgammon is backgammon played through a website, server, or application. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Open Division#

Open Division is a tournament division open to all players, generally the strongest field. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Open Point#

Players use Open Point to describe a point not occupied by two or more opposing checkers and therefore available for legal landing. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Open Tournament#

In backgammon, Open Tournament refers to a tournament that allows entry without a closed qualification requirement. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Opening Game#

Opening Game describes the early stage in which players develop anchors, builders, primes, and attacking chances. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Opening Roll#

The term Opening Roll refers to the first roll of a game, made with one die by each player to determine both the starter and the opening move. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Optional Reroll Rule#

Optional Reroll Rule is a variant rule allowing a player to request or use a limited reroll. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Otter#

Otter is used in some money-game conventions. It is an immediate further redouble after a raccoon. The term belongs to optional cube rules rather than standard match play.

Category:

Outer Board#

The term Outer Board refers to the quadrant containing a player’s seven-point through twelve-point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Outer Checkers#

Outer Checkers describes the three checkers that begin on a player’s eight-point. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Outer Table#

Outer Table is another name for one of the two outer-board quadrants. It refers to the part of the board outside the players’ home boards.

Category:

Outfield#

Outfield is the two outer-board quadrants considered together. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Outside Prime#

Players use Outside Prime to describe a prime built mainly in the outer boards rather than inside a home board. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Over the Board#

Also called: OTB

Over the Board describes something played live in person, rather than online or as analysis. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Overage#

Overage is the portion of a tournament entry or side pool paid above the basic amount or guaranteed prize structure. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Overplay#

Overplay means choosing an unnecessarily aggressive move or continuing a position beyond its practical value. The term describes taking more risk than the position justifies.

Category:

Own a Point#

Also called: Control a Point

The action called Own a Point is to occupy a point with two or more checkers so the other player cannot land there. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Own the Cube#

Also called: Control of the Cube, Cube Ownership, Owner of the Cube, Possession of the Doubling Cube

Own the Cube means to have accepted the last double and therefore hold the exclusive right to redouble. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

P46 terms

Parlay#

The action called Parlay is to roll winnings or an agreed result into a new wager or proposition. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Partial Prime#

In backgammon, Partial Prime refers to a blocking structure of fewer than six consecutive made points. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Partner for the Box#

Players use Partner for the Box to describe a chouette player who temporarily joins the box against the remaining team. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Pass#

Also called: Decline a Double, Drop, Fold, Refuse, Refuse a Double

Pass means to decline a double, end the game, and lose the cube’s value before the offer. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Pay Later#

The action called Pay Later is to postpone an immediate positional cost, accepting the risk that it may be larger later. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Pay Now#

The action called Pay Now is to accept an immediate, known cost to avoid a potentially worse future problem. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Pay-Now-Or-Pay-Later Decision#

Pay-Now-Or-Pay-Later Decision is a choice between taking a positional loss right away or risking a larger loss on later rolls. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Perfecta#

Perfecta is the best possible roll for the position. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Pick and Pass#

Also called: Bump and Pass, Bump and Run, Hit and Pass, Hit and Run

Pick and Pass means hitting a blot and then moving the same checker to safety with the other die. The move attacks without leaving the hitting checker exposed.

Category:

Pigeon#

Pigeon means dated gambling slang for a player viewed as an easy target. This is dated and insulting slang, so it should be labelled clearly rather than used as ordinary teaching language.

Category:

Usage note: Dated and derogatory player slang; label clearly if retained.

Pip#

Pip is one unit of checker movement, or one spot on a die depending on context. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Pip Count#

Also called: Count, Count the Position

Pip Count is the total number of pips all of a player’s checkers must move to bear off. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Plakoto#

Players use Plakoto to describe a Greek Tavli game in which blots are pinned rather than hit and sent to the bar. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Play#

Also called: Checker Play

Players use Play to describe a legal arrangement of checker moves using the rolled dice. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Play Site#

In backgammon, Play Site refers to an online service where users can play backgammon. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Player's Privilege#

In backgammon, Player's Privilege refers to a rule or custom allowing a player to correct or clarify their own action before play continues. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Ply#

Ply is one checker-play turn by one player; two plies make one full pair of turns. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Point#

Also called: Closed Point

Point is one of the 24 triangular spaces on the board, or the scoring unit used in games and matches. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Point Game#

Players use Point Game to describe a strategy based on making and preserving strong points rather than attacking loose checkers. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Point on a Blot#

Also called: POH, Point on Head

Point on a Blot means hitting the other player’s blot with two checkers and making that point at the same time. The move both sends a checker to the bar and closes the landing point.

Category:

Points per Game#

Also called: PPG

Players use Points per Game to describe a performance or scoring average calculated as total points divided by games played. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Poof#

Also called: Puff

Poof means chouette slang for a cube or side action that disappears because a player declines or becomes ineligible. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Portes#

The term Portes refers to the standard backgammon-like game in the Greek Tavli set, generally played without a doubling cube. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Position#

The term Position refers to the complete game state, including checker locations, cube, score, and player on roll. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Position Card#

Position Card is a diagram or written record used to reproduce a specific backgammon position. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Positional Play#

Players use Positional Play to describe a move chosen mainly for long-term structure, flexibility, timing, or game plan rather than an immediate tactic. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Post Mortem#

Post Mortem is discussion and analysis conducted after a game or match. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Post-Crawford#

Post-Crawford refers to any match game played after the Crawford game, when cube use is restored. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Pottle's Law#

Players use Pottle's Law to describe a guideline that the player behind in the race should generally avoid breaking valuable contact unnecessarily. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

PRAT#

In backgammon, PRAT refers to a cube mnemonic: Position, Race, And Threats. If you lead in two or more, consider doubling. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Pre-Crawford#

In backgammon, Pre-Crawford refers to a match game played before either player has reached one-away. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Precision Dice#

Precision Dice describes balanced dice manufactured to tight tolerances for fair live play. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Preclear#

The action called Preclear is to remove spare checkers from a point before being forced to clear it under less favourable conditions. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Premature Burial#

Premature Burial means moving checkers too early onto low home-board points where they lose flexibility. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Premature Roll#

Premature Roll describes rolling before the other player has completed the turn, generally before picking up the dice. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Pressure#

Pressure describes the practical difficulty created by threats, time limits, score, or costly consequences. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Prime#

Also called: Side Prime

In backgammon, Prime refers to a sequence of consecutive made points that blocks opposing checkers. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Prime Fighter#

Prime Fighter is a checker positioned at the edge of a prime, helping contest or escape the blocking structure. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Prime-vs-Prime#

Prime-vs-Prime is a position where each player has a strong prime trapping one or more opposing checkers. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Primed#

Primed refers to trapped behind a prime. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Priming Game#

Priming Game is a game plan focused on building a prime and trapping opposing checkers behind it. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Progressive Consolation#

Progressive Consolation is a consolation format in which players enter at different stages according to when they lost in the main event. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Proposition#

Also called: Prop

Players use Proposition to describe a position or rule set played repeatedly under agreed scoring or odds to test a disagreement or wager. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Proxy#

Also called: Cube Proxy

Proxy is a person or marker authorized to make a cube decision or represent another player in a chouette. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Pure Play#

Players use Pure Play to describe a move that emphasizes building an orderly prime or structure with well-placed builders. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Pure Race#

Also called: Straight Race

In backgammon, Pure Race refers to a position with no remaining contact, so only checker movement and bearoff efficiency matter. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Q6 terms

Quadrant#

Quadrant is one of the board’s four six-point sections. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Quads#

Also called: Girls (The Girls)

The term Quads refers to the roll 4-4. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Quarter Entry#

Players use Quarter Entry to describe a tournament entry purchased for one quarter of the normal fee, often for a partial share of prizes. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Quasi-Random Dice#

Players use Quasi-Random Dice to describe a rollout sequence designed to distribute rolls more evenly than ordinary random sampling. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Quiet Play#

Quiet Play is a low-volatility move that improves structure without creating immediate tactical exchanges. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Quiz Factor#

Quiz Factor refers to how likely a position is to produce a difficult or instructive decision for human players. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

R33 terms

Raccoon#

Raccoon is an immediate redouble by the original doubler after the other player beavers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Race#

The term Race refers to the contest to move all checkers home and bear them off before the other player. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • The Main Game Plans (Checker Play, Doubling Cube)

Race Equity#

Race Equity refers to expected value in a no-contact position based on each side’s winning and gammon chances. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Railroad Tracks#

Railroad Tracks describes two long parallel stacks or lines of checkers that create an inflexible position. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Rake#

Rake is a fee charged by an online or live operator for hosting money play. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Random Error (in a Rollout)#

Random Error (in a Rollout) refers to statistical variation caused by the particular dice sequences sampled in a finite rollout. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Random Seed#

Also called: Seed

Random Seed is a number that initializes a pseudo-random generator and determines its dice sequence. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Rated Match#

In backgammon, Rated Match refers to a match whose result changes the players’ ratings. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Rating#

Players use Rating to describe a numerical estimate of playing strength based on recorded results. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Rating Points#

Rating Points refers to units added to or subtracted from a player’s rating after results. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Ratings Inflation#

In backgammon, Ratings Inflation refers to a rise in the average rating of a player pool without an equivalent rise in true skill. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Ratings Pool#

The term Ratings Pool refers to the set of players whose results contribute to the same rating system. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Ratings System#

Players use Ratings System to describe a method for estimating relative player strength from competition results. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Raw Take Point#

Raw Take Point is the minimum winning chance needed to take when gammons and all future cube action are ignored. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Recirculate#

Recirculate means to allow or invite a checker to be hit so it can re-enter and improve timing or defensive structure. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Recube Vigorish (Vig)#

The term Recube Vigorish (Vig) refers to the extra value of accepting a double because the taker may later redouble. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Redouble#

Also called: Recube

Redouble means to offer another double after previously accepting the cube. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

  • The Doubling Cube (Doubling Cube)
  • Why Is 25% the Basic Take Point When a Double Is Offered? (Doubling Cube)

Reference Position#

Reference Position is a memorized, well-analyzed position used to judge similar decisions. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Resign#

Also called: Claim a Game

The action called Resign is to concede a single game, gammon, or backgammon, subject to the other player’s acceptance. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Response#

Response describes the second roll and reply to the opening play. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Return Shot#

Also called: Comeback Shot

Return Shot is a chance to hit back right away after one of your checkers has been hit. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Robustness#

The term Robustness refers to the ability of a play or position to remain strong across many different future rolls. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Roll#

Roll means to throw the dice, or the pair of values produced. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Roll a Prime#

Also called: Roll a Prime Forward, Walk a Prime

Roll a Prime means to extend the front of a prime while clearing its rear, moving the blocking structure forward. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Roll-Over#

Players use Roll-Over to describe a variant that gives each player a limited right to reroll their own or the other player’s dice. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Rollout#

Also called: Roll Out, Simulation

Players use Rollout to describe a repeated computer or manual simulation used to estimate the equity of candidate plays or cube actions. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • Reading Positions and Engine Analysis (Engines and Analysis)
Related research (1)
  • Sage vs GNU: Additional Details

Root Number#

Players use Root Number to describe a roll that forces the other player’s position to break down or collapse. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Round#

Round is one stage of a tournament in which the scheduled matches are played. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Round Robin Format#

In backgammon, Round Robin Format refers to a format in which every entrant plays every other entrant. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Run#

The action called Run is to move a back checker forward rapidly, generally to escape the other player’s home board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • Opening Play Lab (Opening Play, Checker Play)

Runner#

Also called: Back Man

In backgammon, Runner refers to a back checker that must escape from the other player’s home board, especially one of the two starting on the 24-point. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Running Game#

Running Game is a strategy or phase focused on racing home after contact has ended. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Russian Backgammon#

Russian Backgammon is a variant in which all checkers enter from off the board and both players move in the same direction. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

S66 terms

Safe#

Safe means not currently exposed to being hit. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Safe Play#

Also called: Play Safe, Playing Safe

Players use Safe Play to describe a move that leaves no blots, or only blots with little practical danger. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Safety a Checker#

Also called: Lift

The action called Safety a Checker is to move an exposed checker onto a made point or beyond hitting range. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Safety Up#

Safety Up means covering a blot or moving it out of immediate danger. The goal is to reduce the other player’s chances to hit.

Category:

Sandbag#

Sandbag means to hide one’s true strength, enter an inappropriately weak division, or deliberately lower a rating. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Save a Number#

The action called Save a Number is to preserve a comfortable way to play a specific future number. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Save Backgammon#

The action called Save Backgammon is to escape every checker from the other player’s home board and bar before the other player bears off completely. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Save Gammon#

The action called Save Gammon is to bear off at least one checker before the other player bears off all 15. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Seeded Player#

Seeded Player is a tournament entrant placed deliberately in the draw so top players do not meet too early. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Semiactive Builder#

In backgammon, Semiactive Builder refers to a checker that can make a useful point on some, but not all, relevant rolls. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Semifinalist#

Semifinalist is one of the four players who reaches an elimination tournament’s semifinal round. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Semifinals#

Semifinals is the round that determines the two finalists. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Settlement#

Settlement is an agreement to end a game early for an accepted number of points or amount. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Settlement Limit#

Settlement Limit is a rollout setting that ends a trial when its equity crosses a chosen threshold and assigns a fixed result. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Shake#

Shake means to mix the dice in a cup before rolling. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Shark#

Shark means gambling slang for a strong player who seeks profitable games against weaker opponents. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Shesh Besh#

Shesh Besh is a Turkish form of standard backgammon; the name refers to the roll 6-5. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Shift Gears#

Shift Gears means to change game plans as the position develops. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Shift Points#

Also called: Shift

Shift Points means breaking one made point and using those checkers to make another point, usually nearby. The play changes which part of the board you control.

Category:

Shot#

Players use Shot to describe a possible roll that hits an opposing blot, or the blot’s exposure to such a roll. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Side Pool#

In backgammon, Side Pool refers to an optional extra tournament prize fund entered by some competitors. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Silver Point#

Silver Point means the other player’s four-point, often regarded as the second-best advanced anchor after the five-point. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Simple Direct Shot#

In backgammon, Simple Direct Shot refers to a blot hittable by a single die number but not by combining both dice. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Single Elimination#

Also called: Knockout Tournament

In backgammon, Single Elimination refers to a tournament format in which one loss eliminates a player. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Single Game#

In backgammon, Single Game refers to a normal one-unit win in which the loser has borne off at least one checker. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Single Shot#

Single Shot is one blot exposed to one direct hitting number or route. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Six-Point#

Six-Point is the highest point in a player’s home board, beside the bar. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Slot#

Slot means placing a blot on a point that you hope to cover on a later roll. The play accepts an immediate risk in exchange for a chance to make a valuable point.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • Opening Play Lab (Opening Play, Checker Play)

Slot and Split#

The action called Slot and Split is to slot a home-board point while splitting the back checkers in the same move. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Small Play#

Small Play is a cautious move chosen instead of a stronger but riskier play. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Snake#

Players use Snake to describe a variant in which one player begins with many checkers on the bar and the rest in the other player’s home board. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Snake Eyes#

The term Snake Eyes refers to the roll 1-1. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Snowie#

In backgammon, Snowie refers to an influential commercial neural-network backgammon program first released in the late 1990s. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Solid Prime#

Solid Prime is a prime with no gaps between its made points. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Spare Checker#

Also called: Spare

Spare Checker is a third or later checker on a point that can move without breaking the point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Speed Board#

In backgammon, Speed Board refers to a low, compact bearoff distribution likely to remove two or more checkers on most rolls. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Split#

The action called Split is to separate two checkers on an anchor, generally by advancing one back checker. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • Opening Play Lab (Opening Play, Checker Play)

Splot#

Players use Splot to describe a move that both splits the back checkers and slots a point. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Squeeze#

Squeeze means to leave the other player with legal moves that damage their position or force them to give up a key point. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Stack#

Stack describes four or more checkers piled on one point. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • Opening Play Lab (Opening Play, Checker Play)

Staine's Rule#

Staine's Rule is an optional rule under which doubles are played only twice, like an ordinary two-number roll. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Stake#

Stake is the value wagered on one unit before cube multiplication. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Standard Deviation#

In backgammon, Standard Deviation refers to a statistical measure of rollout uncertainty or spread around the estimated result. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Start a Point#

The action called Start a Point is to place the first checker on a point with the intention of covering it later. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Starting Position#

Also called: Setup

The term Starting Position refers to the standard opening arrangement: 2 checkers on the 24-point, 5 on the 13-point, 3 on the 8-point, and 5 on the 6-point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Stay Back#

The action called Stay Back is to keep one or more checkers in the other player’s home board for contact or timing. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Steam#

Steam means to play recklessly or emotionally after frustration or losses. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Steamer#

Steamer is a player who is steaming or on tilt. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Stop Pot#

In backgammon, Stop Pot refers to a progressive side event in which players may enter at a level and cash out or continue after winning. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Straggler#

In backgammon, Straggler refers to a lone rear checker that still needs to escape or come home. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Strategy#

The term Strategy refers to the long-term plan and positional goals guiding play. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Stretched#

Players use Stretched to describe a position with too few spare checkers and many awkward future rolls. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Strip a Point#

The action called Strip a Point is to remove the last spare checker, leaving exactly two checkers on a made point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Stripped#

Stripped means having made points but few or no spare checkers available to move. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Stroke#

Stroke means to cheat by making a deliberate illegal play or taking another unfair advantage. This term belongs in a rules, ethics, or historical explanation and should not be presented as acceptable conduct.

Category:

Usage note: Include only in an ethics or historical context, not as recommended conduct.

Strong Board#

Players use Strong Board to describe a home board containing several made points, making hits more powerful. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Structural Play#

In backgammon, Structural Play refers to a move that improves long-term checker structure, often by making a strong point. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Suicide Play#

Also called: Hara-Kiri Play, Kamikaze Play

Suicide Play means to leave a checker deliberately available to be hit so it can recirculate and improve timing or defense. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Usage note: Historical jargon. Prefer the neutral term recirculation play in teaching copy.

Hara-Kiri Play: Historical jargon. Prefer the neutral term recirculation play in teaching copy.

Kamikaze Play: Historical jargon. Prefer the neutral term recirculation play in teaching copy.

Svenska Backgammonförbundet (SBGF)#

Svenska Backgammonförbundet (SBGF) is the Swedish Backgammon Federation. Players may see this name in connection with tournaments, membership, or the wider backgammon community.

Category:

Swedish Tables#

Swedish Tables is a Swedish tables-game variant with additional ways to win by forming specified home-board patterns. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Swing#

The term Swing refers to the change in score or equity between two possible outcomes. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Swiss Format#

In backgammon, Swiss Format refers to a tournament system pairing players with similar records over several rounds without immediate elimination. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Swiss-Cheese Formation#

Players use Swiss-Cheese Formation to describe a weak structure with many gaps and few connected made points. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Switch Points#

Switch Points means to give up one made point to make another, often while hitting. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Sydney#

Sydney is slang for the roll 6-1 used to escape a prime, often from the bar. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Systematic Error#

Systematic Error means persistent rollout bias caused by imperfect checker-play or cube-play evaluations. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

T49 terms

Table#

The term Table refers to the full backgammon board, or one of its four quadrants depending on context. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Table Stakes#

Players use Table Stakes to describe a rule limiting losses to the amount placed at risk before the game. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Tables#

In backgammon, Tables refers to a general name for games played on a backgammon-style board, and an English name for Tabula. The term is mainly historical and may not be common in modern play.

Category:

Tabula#

In backgammon, Tabula refers to an ancient Roman tables game played with three dice and movement in one direction. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Tactics#

Tactics means immediate, calculable actions such as hitting, covering, making points, or escaping. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Tailgate#

The action called Tailgate is to begin rolling before the other player has properly completed the turn. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Take#

Also called: Accept a Double

The action called Take is to accept a double and continue the game at twice the previous cube value. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • Why Is 25% the Basic Take Point When a Double Is Offered? (Doubling Cube)

Take Point#

Take Point is the minimum winning chance at which accepting a double is as good as passing. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Related lessons (3)
  • The Doubling Cube (Doubling Cube)
  • What the Cube Is Really Asking (Doubling Cube)
  • Why Is 25% the Basic Take Point When a Double Is Offered? (Doubling Cube)

Take/Drop Proposition#

Take/Drop Proposition refers to repeated play of a position to test whether accepting or passing a double is more profitable. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Takhteh#

Players use Takhteh to describe a Persian form of backgammon. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Tapa#

In backgammon, Tapa refers to a Bulgarian tables game in which opposing blots are pinned rather than hit. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Tavla#

Tavla is the Turkish name for standard backgammon. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Tavli#

Also called: Greek Backgammon

Tavli is the Greek family of tables games, often Portes, Plakoto, and Fevga. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

TD-Gammon#

TD-Gammon means Gerald Tesauro’s pioneering neural-network backgammon program from the early 1990s. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Team#

Team is used in a chouette. It means the captain and crew who play together against the box. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this multiplayer format.

Category:

Technical Play#

In backgammon, Technical Play refers to a checker play driven mainly by concrete tactics and calculation. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Tell#

Tell is an unintended clue about a player’s likely cube response or decision. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Temperature Map#

Temperature Map is a chart showing the equity after each of the 36 possible next rolls. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Tempo#

Tempo is one half-roll of development or timing. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Tempo Move#

Players use Tempo Move to describe a hit made mainly to deprive the other player of time to carry out a threat. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Tempt#

The action called Tempt is to leave a blot intentionally, hoping the other player gives up a valuable point to hit it. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Thorp Count#

In backgammon, Thorp Count refers to an adjusted race count and cube guideline that accounts for checker distribution as well as raw pips. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Three-Point#

Also called: Trey-Point, Trois-Point

Three-Point is the third point in a player’s home board. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Throw#

Also called: Cast

Throw means to release the dice onto the board from a cup or by hand under the rules. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Time#

Time describes the number of rolls or playable pips a structure can preserve before being forced to weaken. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Time Delay#

Players use Time Delay to describe a clock setting that gives a short free interval at the start of each turn before reserve time runs. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Timing#

Timing describes which side will be forced to weaken its structure first as rolls are played. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • The Main Game Plans (Checker Play, Doubling Cube)

Too Good (to Double)#

In backgammon, Too Good (to Double) refers to a position where playing on for a gammon or backgammon is worth more than doubling and receiving a pass. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Too Many Points#

Also called: TMP

In backgammon, Too Many Points refers to an inflexible structure with many made points but too few spare checkers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Touch Down#

Touch Down means to use an intermediate open point while moving one checker with both dice. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Touch Move Rule#

Players use Touch Move Rule to describe a rule requiring a touched checker to be moved and a released legal checker to remain where placed. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Tournament#

Players use Tournament to describe an organized competition with scheduled matches and a method for deciding winners. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Tournament Director#

Also called: TD

Tournament Director is the person responsible for organizing an event and enforcing its rules. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Tourne-Case#

In backgammon, Tourne-Case refers to a historical French race game played with three checkers per player. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Trailer#

The term Trailer refers to the player behind in match score or race. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Transposition#

Transposition refers to reaching the same position through a different order of rolls or plays. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Trap Play#

Players use Trap Play to describe a plan that forces an opponent to leave an anchor, exposing checkers to a closeout and possible gammon. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Trial (of a Rollout)#

Trial (of a Rollout) is one simulated playthrough included in a rollout’s average. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Trice Count#

Trice Count is another name for effective pip count and is associated with Walter Trice. It describes a race count that considers more than the raw number of pips.

Category:

Trice Triangle#

Players use Trice Triangle to describe an efficient bear-in distribution of 7 checkers on the six-point, 5 on the five-point, and 3 on the four-point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Trictrac#

Also called: French Backgammon

Trictrac is a historical French tables game scored for specific plays and formations; the word is also used in French for backgammon. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Truncated Rollout#

Truncated Rollout is a rollout stopped after a fixed search depth, with the remaining positions evaluated rather than played to the end. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Turn#

Turn is one player’s complete sequence of possible cube action, roll, checker play, and dice pickup. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Turn the Corner#

Also called: Clockwise, Move Around the Corner

The action called Turn the Corner is to move from the other player’s outer board into your own outer board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Turner's Formula#

Turner's Formula is a shortcut for estimating match equity from the leader’s score advantage and the trailer’s points needed. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Tutor Mode#

Tutor Mode means software mode that evaluates moves as they are made and warns about mistakes. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.

Category:

Two-Down#

Two-Down is an opening or early play that moves two checkers from the midpoint into the outer board. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Two-Point#

Also called: Deuce-Point, The T.P.

The term Two-Point refers to the second point in a player’s home board, also called the deuce-point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Two-Sided Bearoff Database#

Players use Two-Sided Bearoff Database to describe a database containing results for combinations of both players’ bearoff positions, including cube states. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

U7 terms

Under the Gun#

Players use Under the Gun to describe a blot exposed to several nearby opposing builders and in danger of being pointed on. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Underdog#

The term Underdog refers to the player or side considered less likely to win. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Underplay#

The action called Underplay is to choose an unnecessarily timid or passive play. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Undoubled Gammon#

Players use Undoubled Gammon to describe a gammon won in a game with no cube action. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

United States Backgammon Federation (USBGF)#

United States Backgammon Federation (USBGF) is a nonprofit organization promoting organized backgammon in the United States. Players may see this name in connection with tournaments, membership, or the wider backgammon community.

Category:

Unlimited Game#

Unlimited Game describes cube play without a fixed maximum number of doubles, generally outside match scoring. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Unstack#

The action called Unstack is to move spare checkers away from an overloaded point. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

V8 terms

Variance (of a Rollout)#

Variance (of a Rollout) is the amount of random spread or uncertainty in rollout outcomes. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Variance Reduction#

Variance Reduction describes methods that reduce rollout noise, such as matched dice, quasi-random sequences, or luck adjustment. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Variant#

Variant is a game played on a backgammon board with rules different from standard backgammon. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Vidos#

The term Vidos refers to the Greek name for a cube-using form equivalent to Western backgammon. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.

Category:

Vigorish#

Also called: Vig

Vigorish is a small additional equity effect, such as gammon value or future recube value. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Volatility#

Volatility means how much a position’s equity is likely to change over the next few rolls. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Voluntary Double#

In backgammon, Voluntary Double refers to a normal player-chosen double, as opposed to an automatic opening double. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

Volunteer a Shot#

Volunteer a Shot means to leave a blot now deliberately because being forced to leave one later may be worse. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

W9 terms

Ward Count#

Ward Count is an adjusted pip-count method and cube guideline for pure races. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Wash#

Players use Wash to describe a blitzing play that switches points to hit, or a zero-point settlement depending on context. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Wastage#

Wastage describes expected pip loss during bearoff because rolls cannot be used perfectly. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Related lessons (1)
  • The Main Game Plans (Checker Play, Doubling Cube)

WBA#

WBA stands for World Backgammon Association, the name used by a backgammon organization. Players may see the abbreviation in tournament or community material.

Category:

WBF#

WBF stands for Worldwide Backgammon Federation, an international backgammon organization. Players may see the abbreviation in tournament or community material.

Category:

Weaver Coup#

In backgammon, Weaver Coup refers to a deceptive too-good cube offer made in hopes that the other player incorrectly takes. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.

Category:

Whopper#

Whopper is a very large checker-play or cube error, often more than 0.100 equity. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:

Wisecarver Paradox#

In backgammon, Wisecarver Paradox refers to a race situation where the best checker play correctly provokes a double while an inferior play would not. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.

Category:

Woolseys Law for Doubling#

Woolseys Law for Doubling describes if you are unsure whether the other player has a take or pass, that uncertainty is strong evidence that you should double. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.

Category:

X1 terms

X-22#

X-22 describes the nickname used by backgammon author and champion Paul Magriel. The term is mainly historical and may not be common in modern play.

Category:

Z1 terms

Zone of Attack#

Zone of Attack refers to your one-point through eleven-point, where checkers can support a blitz. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.

Category:
